summary_md:
Abdel-Rahman et al. (2025) swap A* for D* Lite as the low-level single-agent planner inside Conflict-Based Search (CBS), a two-level multi-agent path-finding method. They test it on simulated 3D voxel grids with moving or appearing obstacles. In the paper's Table 2 averages, execution time falls from 5.575 s to 0.04 s and nodes explored fall from 2142 to 250.5, while D* Lite paths come out about 0.8% longer (15.73 vs 15.6). The paper labels that change -0.8% and says optimality is kept. The evidence is thin:
- The number of runs is not reported, and there is no variance or significance test.
- The 5.575 s average does not match its own Table 1, whose values average to 4.575 s.
- The node reduction comes entirely from the 4-neighbour case. With 8 neighbours, D* Lite explores more nodes than A* (198 vs 178).
- The scalability claim rests on one 15-agent case.
- Nothing in the paper concerns legislators, lobbying or social networks.

For Paul's systems, the paper is relevant only to path-finding, as a possible design pattern rather than as evidence. D* Lite earns its speed by reusing earlier search work when edge costs change. None of the built routers do that: the cosponsor route finder, the dashboard recruitment chain and the staffer route search each rebuild every search from scratch on a fixed graph. On a 533-member graph a full recompute is already cheap, so the paper's compute savings do not transfer. Its useful idea is conceptual. When a planned recruitment ask fails or a member's stance changes, the route should be repaired, not abandoned. The dashboard's chain-hold figure currently assumes no rerouting at all. Paul's addendum makes D* Lite and LPA* the operational layer, and this paper is too weak to support that choice on its own.

bearings.paper_claim: Replacing A* with incremental D* Lite inside CBS cuts mean execution time from 5.575 s to 0.04 s (99.2%) and nodes explored from 2142 to 250.5 (88.3%), at about 0.8% longer paths (15.73 vs 15.6). However, the 8-point case explores more nodes with D* Lite (198 vs 178). The number of runs is not reported.
bearings.system_side: The route finder is a static greedy builder on the shared build_P kernel. It reruns build_route from scratch for each of the five lambda values and keeps a Pareto front over cost, expected cosponsors and risk. A per-recruiter whip cap of K=5 is the only shared-resource constraint. MOPBD* is named in the docstring as a concept only. The code does no incremental replanning and no repair when an edge or stance changes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The speedup does not transfer. It was measured on 3D voxel grids with moving obstacles, while this graph has 533 nodes and recomputing it costs very little. What carries over is the idea of repairing a route when a member joins, declines or changes stance, rather than rebuilding it. The K=5 whip cap loosely resembles a CBS conflict over a shared resource, but CBS resolves conflicts between agents competing for space and time, not recruiter bandwidth. Treat the paper as a design pointer only (weak, single-source, unreplicated, UNVERIFIED).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Cosponsor recruitment route finder (Pareto front)|Cosponsor recruitment route finder (Pareto front)]]

bearings.paper_claim: D* Lite reuses earlier search results when costs change, so a route can be repaired instead of recomputed. The authors credit this for faster conflict resolution in dynamic settings, but they report no replanning counts.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.20 (Paul's highlights); Section 3 Eqs. (1)-(3); Section 5 qualitative subsections p.28
bearings.system_side: The dashboard chain uses Dijkstra on -log p. chainHold multiplies activeP over the hops and is documented as P(every ask lands first-try, no reroute), a conservative floor that rerouting could only improve. ASKM=0.07 is an unestimated dial. No reroute-on-failure logic exists.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The extension would need an observed event: a failed ask or a stance move that changes edge probabilities while a campaign is under way. Only then would incremental repair, or simply recomputing the route, give a reroute-aware chain hold. The paper gives no evidence about recruitment success. Edge p values are heuristic kernel outputs, not ask-success probabilities (D-025 wording applies).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Sponsor-to-target max-product path and chain hold|Sponsor-to-target max-product path and chain hold]]

bearings.paper_claim: Incremental planning is not always cheaper. In the 8-point case, D* Lite expanded 198 nodes against A*'s 178. The paper also does not report node counts for single-shot queries on unchanged graphs.
bearings.system_side: The router runs bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 to a virtual sink, plus Yen loopless alternatives. It runs one search per request on a fixed evidence snapshot, with no work caps (exact proof of the optimal route). The latency lane kept one-way Dijkstra without a heuristic and deferred ALT.
bearings.transfer_conditions: D* Lite pays off only when costs change between successive queries on the same graph. Each staffer request starts on a fixed snapshot, so incremental search buys little unless the sidecar starts updating evidence in place between queries. The current design, exact and stateless, has no gap that this paper fills.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-pathfinding#Staffer closeness route search|Staffer closeness route search]]

gaps_exposed: No incremental or repair-based replanning in any built router: cosponsor_route.py, the dashboard buildPath/chainHold, and the staffer routes all recompute from scratch. A route is never updated when a planned ask fails or a stance changes during a campaign.
chainHold explicitly assumes no rerouting, so it understates chain success in any setting where failed hops are re-planned. Nothing models a reroute-aware chain probability.

There is no multi-agent conflict layer. Several recruiters or lobbyists working the same targets at once (overlapping asks, the same member asked by two chains) are handled only by the per-recruiter K cap, not by a CBS-style search over conflicts.
flags: Internal numeric inconsistency: Table 2 reports a CBS-A* mean of 5.575 s, but Table 1's values (8.64 and 0.51) average to 4.575 s. The path-length change is labelled -0.8%, yet D* Lite paths are about 0.8% longer.

The paper is weak as evidence: N is not reported, there is no variance or significance testing, the hardware and seeds are not stated, and scalability rests on a single 15-agent case. The 3-agent and 6-agent figures appear only in the conclusion. Do not quote the 99.2% figure as a general D* Lite speedup.
The node-reduction result reverses in the 8-point neighbour case (198 vs 178), so the claim that D* Lite uniformly reduces nodes explored is false within the paper's own data.

Paul's addendum makes D* Lite and LPA* the operational path-finding layer. This paper does not substantiate that choice for a small, static-per-query legislative graph, and any adoption argument built on it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until it is reproduced independently.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, per-edge volume normalization), and it raises no LDA or reciprocity issues.
paul_alignment: Paul's four highlights, all on the abstract (CBS cost problems, D* Lite as the A* replacement, incremental replanning, faster conflict resolution), match what the paper claims. His component note is still accurate: only the multi-objective concept was built, and cosponsor_route.py does no incremental replanning (verified at fec/engine/cosponsor_route.py:41-71). His note does not record two things. First, the paper's own evidence is thin and partly inconsistent, including the Table 2 vs Table 1 mismatch and the 8-point reversal. Second, on a 533-node graph the compute savings that motivate D* Lite hardly matter. The part worth keeping is reroute-on-failure, which the dashboard chainHold explicitly leaves out. That supports Paul's interest in dynamic replanning as a modeling idea, but not as a performance requirement.

related.why: MOPBD* is the multi-objective D* Lite variant cited as concept-only in cosponsor_route.py. Together with this paper it forms the D* Lite pair behind Paul's operational-layer addendum.
An improved D* Lite for UAV firefighting routes. It is another robotics-only application of the same incremental replanner.
An improved D* Lite for dynamic ship routing in Arctic waters. It shares the same method and the same dynamic-obstacle motivation.
The built recruitment chain runs most-reliable-path Dijkstra on -log p. That paper sets the reliability objective, while this one only addresses replanning compute.
Its review of A*, D* and related pathfinding families gives the broader context for choosing D* Lite over A*.
It is the other speed-oriented path-finding source. It speeds up single-source shortest paths on a static graph, while this paper reuses work when the graph changes.

meta.title: Feasibility of Big Data Analytics to Assess Personality Based on Voice Analysis
meta.venue: Sensors 24(22), 7151 (MDPI, Basel). Received 30 Sep 2024; accepted 4 Nov 2024; published 7 Nov 2024. Open access, CC BY 4.0.

extraction.title: Feasibility of Big Data Analytics to Assess Personality Based on Voice Analysis
extraction.venue: Sensors 24(22), 7151 (MDPI, Basel). Received 30 Sep 2024; accepted 4 Nov 2024; published 7 Nov 2024. Open access, CC BY 4.0.
extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical, exploratory correlational and classification study)
extraction.coverage: Whole file read: all 1517 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\557f30945d46.txt in two chunks (lines 1-1073, then 1074-1517), covering abstract, introduction, methods, results with Tables 3-6, discussion, limitations, supplementary note, and all 62 references. No Paul markup was supplied for this item (the task listed no annotation files), so paul_markup is empty and no annotation file was opened. Metadata hint was correct; the venue field is confirmed as Sensors 24(22), 7151.
extraction.research_question: Three questions stated on p.5 (Introduction, lines 266-286): (1) Are there voice features related to self-reported Big Five scores (externalization)? (2) Are the voice features related to externalization the same as those related to the accuracy of close-other and expert judgments? (3) Can personality dimensions be predicted from voice recorded with ordinary devices in controlled but not restricted speech, so the approach could fit Asynchronous Video Interviews and personnel selection?
extraction.theory: Brunswick lens model as adapted by Scherer (1978): traits are externalized through objectively measurable speech variables (distal cues), perceived by listeners as proximal cues that ground attributions (p.2, lines 80-86). Brown and Bradshaw (1985) three facets: accuracy, externalization, attribution; this study tests externalization and accuracy (p.5, lines 258-265). Big Five framework; the authors also draw on the Cannata et al. (2022) call to join psychological personality-judgment research and personality computing (p.3, lines 156-163). Authors argue speech reveals the self (Allport and Cantril 1934; Allport 1937) (p.5, lines 238-239). No formal hypothesis is stated; the authors describe the study as exploratory.
extraction.data: Unit: individual participant (interview recording). N = 100 female participants, split into Sample 1 (n = 78 female psychology students, aged 18-27, M = 20.18) and Sample 2 (n = 44 female participants, aged 18-54, M = 29.42) (p.5, lines 289-292). NOTE: the two sample sizes sum to 122, not 100; the text does not reconcile this. Recruitment: the first author's School of Psychology participant pool at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, students paid in extra credit (p.5, lines 296-299). Recording period: not stated; the only date is the IRB approval of June 2016 (p.17, lines 1311-1313). Procedure: group session (60-item NEO-FFI, Spanish adaptation), individual interview in the following two weeks, about 7 min per session (p.7, lines 402-410). Audio: WAV, 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit; manually selected open-answer segments, mean 172.8 s (SD 102 s), range 49 s to 15 min; total 4 h 48 min (p.7, lines 414-430). Two different microphones were used for Sample 1 and Sample 2 (p.16). Data available only on request, for privacy reasons (p.17, line 1315). Expert rating subset: N = 20 videos for inter-rater ICC (p.7).
extraction.method: Voice features: the AVEC 2011 emotion feature set extracted with OpenSMILE 2.3, 1941 features (25 energy/spectral LLDs x 42 functionals, 6 voicing LLDs x 32, 25 delta energy/spectral x 23, 6 delta voicing x 19, 10 voiced/unvoiced durations) (p.6, lines 311-323). Analysis 1 (externalization and accuracy): Pearson-type correlation of all 1941 features with each Big Five score from three criteria (self-report, close-other rubric, expert VAS), then reporting the top features per trait in Sample 1 (Table 4). Replication: the top-correlated self-report feature per trait was re-examined in Sample 2 (Section 3.1.6). Analysis 2 (prediction): for each of five traits, the five highest-correlated features were used; scores were binned into low/medium/high at the 25th and 75th percentiles of training data; random forest classifier (scikit-learn, n_estimators = 20, other defaults); leave-one-out with 100 folds (99 train / 1 test). SVM and multiple linear regression were tried but not reported because random forests did better (p.13, lines 1005-1010). Software: Python with Pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn (p.8). The text does not say whether the five features were selected inside each LOO fold or on the full sample; this is a reviewer note, not a stated fact, and it bears on whether the reported accuracies are out-of-sample. The text also does not name the correlation type or any multiple-comparison correction across 1941 features.
extraction.scope: Population: adult female Spanish participants recruited at one Madrid university; Sample 1 is mostly students aged 18-27. Institution: Universidad Autonoma de Madrid (School of Psychology and Polytechnic School of Engineering). Era: collection date not stated; published 2024. Setting: semi-structured interview simulating a job interview (warm-up questions, then self-description, career, and a 15-year future question; p.7 lines 418-424). Sex: all participants are female, which the authors treat as a sample restriction (p.16). Constructs: Big Five self-report, close-other judgments, and zero-acquaintance expert ratings from video plus audio.

key_findings.finding: Close-other ratings correlate with self-report on all Big Five dimensions except Openness. Expert ratings match self-report only for Conscientiousness and Extraversion.
key_findings.numbers: Close-other vs self, significant range 0.32 (Neuroticism) to 0.51 (Extraversion). Expert vs self: 'Responsibility' 0.34 and Extraversion 0.31; both significant, the rest not.

key_findings.finding: Single voice features correlate moderately with personality ratings in Sample 1. The top correlation per trait and criterion is given in Table 4.
key_findings.numbers: Self: Extraversion 0.47 (mfcc_sma[3]_lpgain), Neuroticism 0.37, Openness 0.36, Agreeableness -0.33, Conscientiousness 0.30. Experts: Extraversion 0.48, Neuroticism -0.47, Conscientiousness 0.44, Openness -0.36, Agreeableness 0.35. Close others: Openness -0.41, Agreeableness -0.41, Neuroticism 0.32, Extraversion 0.40 (text says 0.40 in one sentence and 0.41 in the next), Conscientiousness -0.30.

key_findings.finding: Expert ratings showed the strongest voice correlates; the authors read this as expert judgments tracking voice cues more than close-other judgments do.
key_findings.numbers: Largest correlations with acoustic features came from the non-acquainted expert. Expert Extraversion accuracy 60% was the best prediction cell (Table 6).

key_findings.finding: The feature-level correlations did not replicate across samples. Sample 2 (self-report only) gave different features, although of similar magnitude.
key_findings.numbers: Sample 2 top features: Neuroticism mfcc_sma[1]_percentile99.0 r=0.52; Extraversion F0final_sma_quartile3 r=0.46 (p=0.002); Openness mfcc_sma[3]_kurtosis r=0.52; Agreeableness mfcc_sma[2]_skewness r=-0.46 (p=0.002); Conscientiousness mfcc_sma_de[7]_kurtosis r=-0.53. Authors say the results 'did not coincide'.

key_findings.finding: Three-class (low/medium/high) classification from the top-5 voice features gives overall accuracy above the 33% chance rate for most criteria, but not above the 50% majority-class baseline for self-report.
key_findings.numbers: All-cases accuracy (%): Self N 50, E 46, O 46, A 53, C 43. Expert N 57, E 60, O 57, A 56, C 53. Close others N 54, E 57, O 45, A 52, C 54. Chance 33%; a constant central-class prediction gives 50% because the central band holds 50% of cases (p.14).

key_findings.finding: Within-class accuracy is highest for medium-trait cases and lower for low and high cases. Some cells are extreme: the Conscientiousness high-trait cell for self-report is 4.1%.
key_findings.numbers: Medium-trait accuracy ranges 47.4% to 81.1%; examples: close-other Neuroticism medium 76.4%, expert Neuroticism medium 81.1%. Self-report Conscientiousness high 4.1%, Extraversion high 18.2%. Close-other Conscientiousness low 0%, high 64.3%.

key_findings.finding: Expert zero-acquaintance rating reliability was moderate to strong on four dimensions and low on Openness. This rating is the criterion that the authors say voice predicts best.
key_findings.numbers: ICC on N=20 videos: Emotional Adjustment 0.70, Extraversion 0.73, Agreeableness 0.74, Conscientiousness 0.82, Openness 0.23. Experts discussed disagreements and re-rated Openness.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion's numbers do not match the Results. It says the highest trait correlations were Neuroticism 0.38 and Extraversion 0.40, and that the predictions range 0.3 to 0.4. Results and Table 4 report 0.47 to 0.48 for Extraversion.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.1 (lines 45-47); Discussion p.14 (lines 1129-1132); Results p.8-10 (lines 459-460, 466, 475)
key_findings.numbers: Discussion: N 0.38, E 0.40. Results: E 0.47 (self), 0.48 (expert). Text claims all correlations p<0.001 with a maximum of 0.50, but Table 4 shows p = 0.0013, 0.002, 0.004 and 0.01 for some cells and a maximum of 0.48.

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the voice results with facial-expression work and conclude voice alone is more limited; they call personality prediction a multimodal task.
key_findings.numbers: Voice best case about 60% accuracy vs over 75% for facial-expression work by Gavrilescu (ref 56, cited as [56]).

limitations: Sample: 100 participants, all female, mostly psychology students (age 18-27 in Sample 1). Authors say the group is homogeneous in age and personality, so extreme trait values are unlikely, limiting external validity (p.16).
Effect sizes are moderate and may not hold in larger or more varied samples; the authors say they should be read cautiously (p.16).
No cross-cultural sampling; the authors say cultural norms may change how traits are externalized through voice (p.16).

Confounders: noise in some recordings; two different microphones for Sample 1 and Sample 2, which the authors say may explain the lack of replication; colds, fatigue and emotional state could act as latent variables (p.16).
Only vocal aspects were analyzed. Fluency (pauses, discontinuities), morphology/syntax, conversational behavior, facial expression, body language and movement were not (p.17).
Feature interpretability is weak: most top features are MFCC or LPC coefficients whose meaning is unclear, and the top features did not replicate across samples (pp.12-15).

No explicit power analysis. The authors say N = 100 gives 80% power for correlations near 0.2 (p.5, lines 300-304). Many features (1941) raise the risk of spurious correlation; the authors used two samples to check consistency (p.5).
Expert Openness reliability was low (ICC 0.23 on 20 videos) (p.7).

Internal inconsistencies found in the text, not reconciled by the authors: Sample sizes 78 + 44 = 122 vs N = 100; Discussion correlation values (0.38/0.40) vs Results (0.47/0.48); Extraversion close-other r given as both 0.40 and 0.41; 'all p < 0.001' vs Table 4 p-values up to 0.01; 'one of two experts' vs both experts rating videos (p.7).
Data are available only on request for privacy reasons, so the results cannot be reproduced from the paper alone (p.17).

Prediction set-up: the text does not say whether feature selection (top-5 by correlation) was done inside each leave-one-out fold; this must be checked before accepting the 43-60% accuracies as out-of-sample.
measures: Big Five self-report: NEO-FFI, 60-item Spanish adaptation (Cordero et al. 2008), completed in a group session (p.7).

Close-other judgments: 3-point (low/medium/high) rubric for 5 dimensions, completed by a relative or close friend; adapted from the NEO-FFI manual summary sheet (p.7; rubric in Supplementary Materials).

Expert zero-acquaintance ratings: 15 cm visual analog scale per Big Five dimension, scored as cm from the 0 mark, based on watching the full video (p.7). Two experienced PhD assessors (one female, one male; over 25 years of experience); calibrated to 100% agreement on cues before rating.
Inter-rater ICC on 20 videos: Emotional Adjustment 0.70, Extraversion 0.73, Agreeableness 0.74, Conscientiousness 0.82, Openness 0.23 (p.7).
Voice features: OpenSMILE AVEC 2011 emotion set, 1941 functionals (LLDs, deltas, voicing, durations) (p.6, Tables 1-2).
Dependent variable for prediction: low/medium/high classes at training-set 25th and 75th percentiles (p.13).
references_of_note: Ambady and Rosenthal 1992, Psychol. Bull. 111:256 (ref 3): thin-slice meta-analysis, overall accuracy 0.39 in zero-acquaintance predictions of outcomes. Relevant to the persuasion/accuracy theme.

Mairesse, Walker, Mehl and Moore 2007, J. Artif. Intell. Res. 30:457 (ref 14): automatic recognition of personality from linguistic cues in conversation and text. Closest text-measurement precedent in the reference list.
Van Zant and Berger 2020, J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 118:661 (ref 23): 'How the voice persuades'; paralinguistic cues (pitch, volume) enhance persuasion. Only persuasion-related work the paper cites.
Breil, Osterholz, Nestler and Back 2021 (ref 24): review of 32 studies, up to 39 non-verbal cues, correlations with Big Five traits.
Cannata et al. 2022, Technol. Mind Behav. 3:1 (ref 27): framework linking psychological and AI personality research; the paper's stated bridge.
Hickman et al. 2022, J. Appl. Psychol. 107:1323 (ref 50): reliability, validity and generalizability of automated video-interview personality assessments.
Koutsoumpis et al. 2024, Comput. Hum. Behav. 154:108128 (ref 49): audio signals predict self-report and expert-rated traits in asynchronous video interviews.
Hosoda, Stone-Romero and Coats 2003 (ref 60): meta-analysis of physical attractiveness effects on job outcomes; cited for recruiter attribution bias.
Youyou, Kosinski and Stillwell 2015, PNAS 112:1036 (ref 57): computer-based personality judgments more accurate than human judgments.
Eyben et al. 2010 (ref 39, OpenSMILE) and Schuller et al. 2011 (ref 38, AVEC 2011 feature set): the feature pipeline used.
Mohammadi and Vinciarelli 2012, IEEE Trans. Affect. Comput. 3:273 (ref 41): automatic personality perception from prosodic features; Speaker Personality Corpus source.
Pennebaker and King 1999 (ref 59) and Argamon et al. 2005 (ref 58): lexical and linguistic-style predictors of personality; the text-based tradition the authors contrast with voice.
Marrero et al. 2022, Acta Psychol. 230:103740 (ref 21): voice samples predict self-reported traits (about 10% of variance).

short_quotes.quote: Voice features are related to the externalization of individuals' personality characteristics.

extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is cross-sectional: correlations between acoustic features and three personality criteria (Sample 1, with Sample 2 as a replication for self-report), then leave-one-out random-forest classification on N = 100. No instrument, quasi-experiment or manipulation. Out-of-sample validity depends on whether feature selection was inside each fold, which the text does not state.
extraction.theory_note: The paper treats personality as externalized through vocal cues and perceived by judges. Accuracy and externalization are kept separate (Brown and Bradshaw 1985).

summary_md:
Rubio, Aguado, Toledano and Fernandez-Gallego (Sensors 2024) recorded about 7-minute mock job interviews with Spanish women, nearly all students. They extracted 1,941 OpenSMILE AVEC-2011 acoustic functionals and correlated them with Big Five scores from three sources: NEO-FFI self-report, close-other ratings and zero-acquaintance expert ratings. In Sample 1 (n=78), the best single feature reached r of about 0.30-0.48 per trait. Expert ratings tracked voice most closely (E 0.48, N -0.47). The paper also says N=100, but its two samples add to 122.

The key result is negative: the top features did not replicate in Sample 2 (n=44). The authors suggest a microphone change may explain this. For prediction, the top five features fed a random forest that sorted people into low, medium or high on each trait, scored by leave-one-out. Self-report accuracy was 43-53%, no better than the 50% you get by always guessing "medium". Expert ratings did best, at 53-60%. The paper never says whether the top five features were chosen inside each fold, so even those figures may be optimistic. The Discussion's numbers also contradict the Results (0.38/0.40 vs 0.47/0.48).

For Melange, the paper backs the audio lane's existing verdict rather than reopening it. The lane uses a related toolkit (eGeMAPS v02 from openSMILE), and its audio Neuroticism (N) pilot was a MISS. Audio is display-only, and the engine never reads it. The paper adds two concrete cautions. First, a change of channel (microphone or venue) can wipe out feature-level findings. Second, a sample of one sex hides the sex confound in pitch variability. Melange measured that confound, but the fix is not on the live branch (see flags).

bearings.paper_claim: Single-feature voice-trait correlations of r about 0.30-0.48 in Sample 1 (n=78) did not replicate in Sample 2 (n=44, self-report only): different top features, which the authors call results that 'did not coincide'. They blame the switch between two microphones, plus noise, colds and fatigue. Voice alone peaks at about 60% three-class accuracy, against over 75% in facial-expression work, so they call personality prediction a multimodal task.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1.6, pp.12-13 (lines 981-998); Limitations p.16; Discussion p.14 (lines 1138-1144)
bearings.system_side: The lane extracts eGeMAPS v02 (88 openSMILE functionals) per verified solo clip, pools them per member weighted by duration, then z-scores and winsorizes at +/-5. Channel (studio, remote or telephone) is recorded as uncontrolled. There is a large venue confound in disfluency (about 26 per 1k words live vs 0.22 per 1k on NPR). The engine and ranks never read audio, and the audio N look was spent and MISSed on 2026-08-25.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's sample is all female, Spanish, mostly aged 18-27, with self-report criteria. Members of Congress are mixed-sex and older, recorded across many outlets, with no self-report criterion. The transfer is the methodological lesson: feature-level findings break when the recording channel changes. The effect sizes do not transfer. The Melange corpus has much more channel heterogeneity than two microphones, so the instability risk is larger here, which reinforces display-only.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: Prediction: the 5 features most correlated with each trait were picked from 1,941, scores were binned at the 25th/75th percentiles, and a random forest (20 trees) was scored by leave-one-out on N=100. Self-report accuracy was N 50, E 46, O 46, A 53, C 43%, against a 50% majority-class baseline. Expert accuracy was 53-60%. The paper does not say whether feature selection ran inside each fold, and it applies no multiple-comparison correction across 1,941 correlations.
bearings.system_side: The audio pilot does no univariate pre-selection. Ridge regression uses all 88 features, alpha is tuned by GridSearch inside each outer fold, and 5-fold CV is repeated over 5 seeds. A permutation null with the same estimator sets the noise floor. The ES cross-modal re-test likewise uses all 88 features with nested CV and 5000 label permutations, and no analyst sign choices. That re-test gave held-out r=+0.208 (perm p=.0002) at the Melange N; it is a single path and stays UNVERIFIED as a trait claim.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Melange's design already guards against the leakage this paper may contain, so Rubio's accuracies cannot be used as a bar or prior for Melange looks. The overall rates sit at or below the 50% majority baseline for self-report, and selection may have run outside the folds. At most they say the expected effect is small: about r 0.3-0.5 for the best single feature, before correcting for selection across 1,941 features. That fits Melange's MISS at N=90.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: All 100 participants are female. The authors list this as a limit on generalization, and it also removes sex as a confound in pitch features. The paper never estimates how sex affects F0-based features.
bearings.system_side: Melange measured r(sex=F)=-0.266 (d=-0.944, 1,324 clips / 309 members) on F0semitone stddevNorm. Commit 4193f0140 changed pitch_variability_raw to the plain semitone SD (stddevNorm*amean) and barred stddevNorm on its own. That commit is NOT an ancestor of HEAD (git merge-base --is-ancestor returns false). The live file still emits stddevNorm alone and labels the metric without the bar.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A same-sex study gives no evidence that pitch-variability effects survive in a mixed-sex legislature. Any pitch-based descriptor in Melange needs sex conditioning or the de-normalized SD. Melange's own Salam-2022 check found pace and volume_dynamics free of sex effects; pitch variability and jitter are not.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-audio-speech#eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates|eGeMAPS prosody and Whisper disfluency rates]]

bearings.paper_claim: The strongest voice correlates come from zero-acquaintance expert ratings made from video plus audio (E 0.48, N -0.47, C 0.44), not from self-report. The authors read this as voice tracking what a listener attributes more than the person's self-view. Self-other agreement on Openness was not significant, and expert Openness ICC was 0.23.
bearings.paper_location: Table 3-4 pp.8-12; Discussion pp.14-16 (lines 1155-1160, 1225-1228); Section 2.2.2 p.7
bearings.system_side: The persona channel models the projected persona that a lobbyist meets, built from LLM cue classification of text. The audio descriptors are written as listener-facing descriptions in narrative paragraphs and make no trait claims.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This loosely supports framing audio as a perceived persona rather than a trait. The expert-rating result rests on two raters and 20 ICC videos in a non-political, all-female sample, so it does not validate any Melange persona weight. PERSONA_W stays an owner ruling.

gaps_exposed: The sex-confound fix for pitch_variability_raw (stddevNorm*amean, commit 4193f0140, 2026-08-21) is not on the live branch. fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:217 still emits stddevNorm alone, a metric Melange itself measured as sex-loaded (r=-0.266). This finding is UNVERIFIED under DE-062: one path only (git ancestry plus a file read).

There is no explicit channel or microphone stratum. Rubio's non-replication across two microphones suggests eGeMAPS features should be checked for stability within member across recording channels, or z-scored within venue. The brain lists channel as uncontrolled.

Melange has no test of whether vocal descriptors match how listeners perceive members, as opposed to self-reported traits. That is where Rubio found the strongest signal (expert ratings). The system has no rater panel for audio-perceived persona.
flags: Do not cite Rubio's 43-60% accuracies as evidence that voice predicts personality. For self-report they do not beat the 50% majority baseline. Fold placement of feature selection is unstated. There is no multiple-comparison correction across 1,941 features.

The paper is internally inconsistent: N=100 vs 78+44=122; Discussion r 0.38/0.40 vs Results 0.47/0.48; 'all p<0.001' vs Table 4 p values up to 0.01. Quote figures only from the Results tables, with the sample named.

Every figure comes from a homogeneous Spanish sample of 100 women in mock job interviews, with a recording date not stated. Mark any transfer to members of Congress as UNSTRATIFIED by sex and channel.
The audio N route is closed (look spent 2026-08-25). This paper does not justify reopening it, and a new audio-trait look would need a fresh pre-registration under the single-look discipline.

The missing-fix finding (4193f0140 not an ancestor of HEAD) is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). It is reported here, not repaired: the repo is read-only for this task.
paul_alignment: Paul's notes favor non-textual channels (audio, video, image) and ask for a framework that handles the 'contextual or auditory constraints' of a format (Ramey). Rubio gives that concern concrete content: one microphone change was enough to break feature-level replication, and voice alone reached only about 60% at best. Overall, the evidence sides with the system's conclusion (audio is display-only; the audio N pilot MISSed) more than with an expectation that voice will yield trait scores. Paul's note is not stale so much as left open: it asks for a framework, and the system has answered with display-only plus reliability ranking (pause .92 > pace .86 > volume .85 >> pitch). Paul did not annotate this paper.

related.why: Rubio cites Marrero (ref 21): voice samples explain about 10% of self-reported trait variance. Both test the same voice-to-self-report question, with similarly modest effects.

Same target: automatic recognition of self-reported personality. Melange's Salam-2022 check on sex-clean pace and volume, and on sex-loaded pitch variability, fills in the sex-confound question that Rubio's all-female sample cannot answer.
Audio as data for political research: alignment, features and classification pitfalls. Rubio's non-replication across microphones is a concrete case of those pitfalls.
Vocal pitch in congressional speech measures emotional intensity, not trait. It is the political-domain counterpart to Rubio's lab interview setting.
Expert ratings of legislators' traits (Personality on the Hill) play the same role as Rubio's zero-acquaintance expert criterion, which tracked voice most closely.
Ramey measures elite personality from the words in speech; Rubio measures it from the acoustics. Rubio sets the voice channel against the lexical tradition.
A review of threats in personality computing. Rubio's selection-leakage ambiguity and failed replication are examples of the reproducibility problems it covers.

meta.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
meta.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113, 117-143

extraction.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
extraction.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113, 117-143
extraction.document_type: Empirical journal article: three-study scale development and validation (measurement instrument)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 4,130 lines of the extracted text (printed pp. 1-79), covering front matter, abstract, introduction, Study 1, Study 2, Study 3, general discussion, limitations, conclusion, references, Tables 1-11, Figures 1-4 (captions and surrounding text only; figure graphics are not in the text file), appendix (60-item form) and scoring key. Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied for this PDF, so paul_markup is empty. Domain check: the paper contains no content on lobbying, social networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text-as-data measurement. "Nomological network" is a construct-validity term (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955), not a social network. Lexical sourcing of items from trait adjectives and IPIP phrases (Study 1, Phase 2) is the only text-related element.
extraction.theory: Big Five trait structure (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Negative Emotionality, Open-Mindedness) with a hierarchical facet level. Bandwidth-fidelity tradeoff (Cronbach and Gleser, 1957; John, Hampson, and Goldberg, 1991): broad traits predict broadly, narrow facets predict specifically. Facets are chosen as factor-pure (anchor the domain) plus complementary (broaden it). Acquiescent responding is a response style that biases reliability, structure and validity unless items are content-balanced (Jackson and Messick, 1958).
extraction.research_question: Can a brief Big Five inventory be built with a robust hierarchical structure (three facets per domain), balanced true-keyed and false-keyed content to control acquiescence, and greater bandwidth, fidelity and predictive power than the original 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI), while keeping the BFI's focus, clarity and brevity?
extraction.data: Study 1 (item development): N = 1,137 members of the Eugene-Springfield Community Sample (Oregon adults), age 18-89 (M = 49.64, SD = 13.02), 52.9% female; 641 completed the BFI; 1,131 completed at least one trait-adjective list (885 adjectives); 995 completed at least one IPIP list (2,552 IPIP items); 401 completed all 12 IPIP lists. Study 2 (scale construction): N = 1,000 adults from personalitylab.org (500 men, 500 women), age 18-77 (M = 29.25, SD = 12.17), 79% US residents; all rated a 110-item pool. Study 3 (validation): internet sample N = 1,000 personalitylab.org visitors (500 men, 500 women), age 18-74 (M = 28.73); student sample N = 470 psychology students at a large public university (146 men, 313 women, 11 unreported), age 16-49 (M = 21.68). Subsamples: 8-week retest n = 110; peer reports n = 184 (60% friends, 30% romantic partners); behavioral self-reports (Schwartz values, about two weeks later) n = 439; psychological well-being n = 179; other Big Five measures (Mini-Markers, BFAS, NEO PI-R, NEO-FFI) n = 438. Unit: individual respondent. Study period: not stated in the text. Note: the student sample is 470 in the text but 459 in the gender breakdown of Table 5.
extraction.method: Rational-empirical scale development in three studies. Study 1: three facets per domain chosen as one factor-pure facet plus two complementary facets (pp. 15-18); marker adjectives correlated against 885 adjectives, 2,552 IPIP items and 44 BFI items to find item content (pp. 18-19); preliminary pool of 110 items (44 original, 19 revised, 47 new) with at least three true-keyed and three false-keyed items per facet (p. 19). Study 2: rational review plus convergent and discriminant correlations with preliminary scales, and balanced keying, to select 60 items (four per facet, 15 facets, 5 domains of 12 items) (pp. 21-22); PCA with varimax rotation on the development sample, which the authors flag as possibly favorably biased (p. 22). Study 3 (independent samples): alpha and retest reliability; self-peer correlations; PCAs of raw and within-person-centered items; five-component varimax solutions for domains and facets with Tucker-type congruence; CFA of five model sets per domain (single domain, single domain plus acquiescence, positive/negative items, three facets, three facets plus acquiescence; acquiescence factor loadings fixed at 1 and uncorrelated with substantive factors); monotrait-heteromethod and heterotrait correlations with other Big Five measures; IRT test information comparisons with the BFI; and regressions predicting 20 self- and peer-reported criteria from BFI domains, post hoc BFI facets, BFI-2 domains and BFI-2 facets, with facets chosen by forward regression (inclusion p < .01, maximum three predictors) (pp. 22-38).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is an observational psychometric validation. Acquiescence is handled three ways: content-balanced keying (equal true- and false-keyed items per scale), within-person centering of items (p. 10, p. 30), and modeling acquiescence as a latent method factor in CFA (p. 32-33). Validity evidence is correlational (convergent, discriminant, self-peer, and criterion correlations and regressions). No causal or quasi-experimental design is used.
extraction.scope: Population: adults in economically developed English-speaking nations, mainly young or middle-aged and mostly with at least high-school education (Study 1 community sample from Oregon; Studies 2-3 volunteers from personalitylab.org, an online feedback site; Study 3 student sample from one public university). Not representative; the authors say population norms are still needed (p. 46). Era: not stated in the text. Institution: not applicable beyond the named samples. Measure scope: Big Five domains plus 15 facets, 60 items, 10 minutes or less.

key_findings.finding: Hierarchical model: 15 facets (three per Big Five domain) selected as one factor-pure plus two complementary facets per domain. Extraversion: Sociability, Assertiveness, Energy Level. Agreeableness: Compassion, Respectfulness, Trust. Conscientiousness: Organization, Productiveness, Responsibility. Negative Emotionality: Anxiety, Depression, Emotional Volatility. Open-Mindedness: Intellectual Curiosity, Creative Imagination, Aesthetic Sensitivity.
key_findings.location: Study 1, Phase 1, pp. 15-18; Table 1, p. 61; Conclusion of Study 1, p. 20
key_findings.numbers: 15 facets; 3 per domain; 110-item preliminary pool (44 original, 19 revised, 47 new)

key_findings.finding: Final BFI-2: 60 items, four per facet, 12 per domain. Reliability in the scale-development sample (Study 2): domain alphas .87 E, .83 A, .88 C, .91 N, .84 O; facet alphas .65-.84, mean .76. First PCA: all 15 facets loaded most strongly on their intended component (primary loadings at least .73, M = .80); all 60 items loaded most strongly on the intended component (at least .41, M = .60).
key_findings.numbers: 60 items; domain alpha .83-.91; facet alpha .65-.84 (M = .76); facet primary loadings >= .73 (M = .80); item primary loadings >= .41 (M = .60)

key_findings.finding: Study 3 reliability: all five domain alphas were at least .83 internet and .85 student; eight-week retest of domains was at least .76 (student). Facet alphas ranged .66-.85 in each sample (mean .76 internet, .77 student); facet retest .66-.83 (mean .73).
key_findings.location: Study 3, Reliability section, p. 28; Tables 2-3, pp. 62-63
key_findings.numbers: domain alpha >= .83 (internet), >= .85 (student); domain retest >= .76; facet alpha .66-.85; facet retest mean .73

key_findings.finding: Discrimination: absolute correlations among domains averaged .20 (internet) and .24 (student). Within-domain facet correlations averaged .53 (internet) and .55 (student), versus absolute between-domain facet correlations of .16 and .19.
key_findings.location: Study 3, pp. 28-29; Table 2, p. 62; Table 3, p. 63
key_findings.numbers: domain intercorrelation mean |r| = .20/.24; within-domain facet r = .53/.55; between-domain facet |r| = .16/.19

key_findings.finding: Self-peer agreement (student sample, peer n = 184): domain agreement .42-.69 (mean .56) versus absolute discriminant mean .11. Facet agreement .27-.73 (mean .49), within-domain discriminant mean .32, between-domain discriminant mean .10. Thirteen of 15 self-reported facets and 14 of 15 peer-reported facets had their strongest correlation with the corresponding facet on the other rater's side.
key_findings.numbers: domain agreement mean r = .56; facet agreement mean r = .49; 13/15 and 14/15 strongest-match counts

key_findings.finding: Acquiescence: PCA of 60 raw items gave six components above the scree line (Big Five plus an acquiescence component) in both samples. Within-person centering removed the extra component. Five varimax components of centered items reproduced the Big Five, with primary loadings averaging .62 (internet) and .61 (student); congruence with raw-item components was .97 or higher.
key_findings.location: Study 3, Domain-level structure, pp. 30-31; Figure 1, p. 73; Table 6, pp. 66-67
key_findings.numbers: raw-item PCA: 6 components vs 5 after centering; primary loadings M = .61 (internet raw), .60 (student raw), .62 (internet centered), .61 (student centered); congruence >= .97

key_findings.finding: Facet-level acquiescence: the PCA of 15 facet scales showed only five components above the scree line (first five eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32 in the internet sample, then 0.56 or lower), so the content-balanced facets did not produce an acquiescence component. Facet primary loadings were at least .73 (M = .81, internet) and at least .67 (M = .79, student), with congruence .98 or higher.
key_findings.numbers: 5 components above scree; eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32; facet primary loadings >= .73 (M = .81) and >= .67 (M = .79)

key_findings.finding: Confirmatory factor analysis within domains: a single-domain model fit poorly (CFI <= .805 internet, <= .800 student). Adding acquiescence or separating positive and negative items gave a large fit gain for Agreeableness but still poor fit (CFI <= .876 / .850). The three-facet model fit acceptably or nearly acceptably for E, C, N, O (CFI >= .902 / .895), and the three-facets-plus-acquiescence model fit acceptably for all domains (CFI >= .930 / .932).
key_findings.numbers: single-domain CFI <= .805 / .800; three facets CFI >= .902 (internet) / .895 (student) for E, C, N, O; three facets plus acquiescence CFI >= .930 / .932; RMSEA about .054-.075 for the best model per domain (Agreeableness .054 / .058)

key_findings.finding: Convergence with other Big Five measures (student sample): monotrait-heteromethod correlations averaged .92 with the original BFI, .82 with the BFAS, .80 with Mini-Markers, .75 with NEO-FFI and .72 with NEO PI-R; absolute heterotrait-heteromethod correlations averaged .21. Gains over the original BFI were largest for Agreeableness (.75 vs .70) and Open-Mindedness (.76 vs .72).
key_findings.numbers: convergent r: BFI .92, BFAS .82, Mini-Markers .80, NEO-FFI .75, NEO PI-R .72; heterotrait mean |r| = .21; A .75 vs .70; O .76 vs .72

key_findings.finding: Facet convergence: 53 BFI-2 facet correlations with same-domain BFAS aspects and NEO PI-R facets were at least .50, and each facet had a distinctive profile (for example, Assertiveness with BFAS Assertiveness r = .85; Organization with Order r = .74; Depression with Withdrawal r = .77).
key_findings.location: Study 3, Facet-level associations, pp. 35-36; Figure 3, pp. 74-76 (N = 438)
key_findings.numbers: 53 correlations >= .50; r = .85, .74, .77 as listed

key_findings.finding: Information: IRT test information was similar in shape for BFI and BFI-2 domains, but the BFI-2 gave about 55% more information on Negative Emotionality, 15% on Extraversion, 29% on Agreeableness, 12% on Open-Mindedness and 11% on Conscientiousness.

Predictive power: across 20 self- and peer-reported criteria, mean R-squared was .25 for BFI domains, .27 for post hoc BFI facets, .27 for BFI-2 domains and .33 for BFI-2 facets. Entering BFI-2 facets after BFI domains added significant variance for 14 of 20 criteria.
key_findings.location: Nomological network section, pp. 37-39; Table 11, p. 72; Figure 4, p. 77; footnote 7, pp. 38-39
key_findings.numbers: mean R2 = .25 (BFI domains), .27 (post hoc BFI facets), .27 (BFI-2 domains), .33 (BFI-2 facets); 14/20 criteria with significant incremental R2 for BFI-2 facets

key_findings.finding: Domain-level criterion patterns were nearly identical between BFI and BFI-2: column-vector correlations of zero-order correlations across 20 criteria averaged .98, as did standardized coefficients. Associations were slightly stronger for BFI-2 domains, giving higher explained variance.
key_findings.numbers: column-vector r = .98 (zero-order and standardized coefficients)

key_findings.finding: Facet-level predictors were distinct and conceptually meaningful. Examples (Table 10, r/beta): Benevolence predicted by Compassion (.47/.29) and Trust (.45/.28); Self-direction by Intellectual Curiosity (.44/.39); Stress resistance by Emotional Volatility (-.47/-.32) and Anxiety (-.46/-.28); Positive relations by Depression (-.53/-.38).
key_findings.numbers: see Table 10 r/beta values listed

key_findings.finding: Acquiescence index: averaging all 60 raw items without reversing false-keyed items gives a yea-saying or nay-saying index (range 1.00 to 5.00). The authors propose the BFI-2 for studying acquiescence itself.
key_findings.numbers: range 1.00-5.00 across 60 items

limitations: Samples are mostly young or middle-aged adults with at least high-school education; population norms are not yet available (p. 46). Reliability and validity among older adults and less-educated respondents are untested (pp. 46-47). The BFI-2's revisions for easier wording have not been directly tested for improved measurement among younger or less-educated respondents (p. 46).
All participants lived in economically developed English-speaking nations, so cross-cultural structure and correlates are untested (pp. 46-47).

Brevity forces exclusions. Domain-level: traits beyond the Big Five and constructs such as characteristic adaptations and narrative identity are excluded (p. 47). Facet-level: behavioral Open-Mindedness facets and peripheral facets such as excitement-seeking, modesty, deliberation and impulsivity are excluded (pp. 47-48). Item-level: anger/irritability content is measured only indirectly through Emotional Volatility (p. 48).

Study 2 facet and domain reliability and PCA results come from the same sample used to refine the item pool, so they may be favorably biased by capitalization on chance; the authors therefore emphasize Study 3 (p. 22).

Study 3 internet and student samples are self-selected (online feedback-seekers and course participants). The student sample is strongly gendered (313 women, 146 men) and the internet sample reports higher Open-Mindedness and Negative Emotionality than students (p. 29-30).

The 4-item facet scales have modest reliability (facet alphas .66-.85), and the authors note some Schwartz-value criteria have low alphas (.27-.70), which they retained as an a priori criterion set (p. 26-27).
Self-reported behavioral and psychological criteria come from single-method self-report, and peer reports are from a subsample of acquaintances (n = 184).

The authors recommend simple item aggregation for new studies. Regression-derived equations for switching from BFI to BFI-2 are available from the first author (footnote 3, p. 34), not reported in the text.
measures: BFI-2: 60 items, 5-point agree-disagree scale; 15 facets (4 items) and 5 domains (12 items); balanced true- and false-keyed items; scoring key in Appendix pp. 78-79.
Original Big Five Inventory (BFI; 44 items), used for comparison.
Big Five Mini-Markers (Saucier, 1994): 40 unipolar adjectives on 9-point scale.
Big Five Aspect Scales (BFAS; DeYoung et al., 2007): 100 items, 10 aspects.
NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (NEO PI-R; 240 items; 30 facets) and NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI; 60 items).
Behavioral self-reports (Bardi and Schwartz, 2003): 80 items on the previous six months, within-person centered, aggregated into 10 Schwartz values scales (alpha .27-.70).
Psychological Well-Being Scales (Ryff, 1989): 84 items, six 14-item aspects (alpha .85-.92).
Peer-reported criteria (English et al., 2012): social connectedness (4 items), likability (2), stress resistance (5), positive affect (2).
Trait-descriptive adjectives (885, from Goldberg, 1992; Saucier, 1994, 1997) and IPIP items (2,552, Goldberg, 1999; Goldberg et al., 2006) used for item development in Study 1.
references_of_note: Hofstee, De Raad and Goldberg (1992), Integration of the Big Five and circumplex approaches (AB5C; factor-pure facet logic).
Costa and McCrae (1995), Domains and facets: hierarchical personality assessment using the NEO PI-R (hierarchical bandwidth-fidelity approach).
DeYoung, Quilty and Peterson (2007), Between facets and domains: 10 aspects of the Big Five (aspect-level structure, BFAS basis).
Ashton, Jackson, Paunonen, Helmes and Rothstein (1995), The criterion validity of broad factor scales versus specific facet scales (bandwidth-fidelity evidence).
Paunonen and Ashton (2001), Big Five factors and facets and the prediction of behavior (facet-level prediction of behavior).
Ozer and Benet-Martinez (2006), Personality and the prediction of consequential outcomes (review of trait prediction).
John, Hampson and Goldberg (1991) and Cronbach and Gleser (1957), bandwidth-fidelity tradeoff.
Soto and John (2009a), Ten facet scales for the Big Five Inventory (post hoc BFI facets, direct precursor).
Soto, John, Gosling and Potter (2008), developmental psychometrics of Big Five self-reports and acquiescence.
Rammstedt and Farmer (2013), impact of acquiescence on personality structure (lower education).

summary_md:
Soto and John build the BFI-2, a 60-item self-report Big Five inventory. It has 15 facets, three per domain, and each facet has four items with equal numbers of true-keyed and false-keyed items. Validation in independent internet (N = 1,000) and student (N = 470) samples gives domain alphas of at least .83 and facet alphas of .66 to .85. Self-peer agreement averages .56 at the domain level and .49 at the facet level (peer n = 184). Convergence with other Big Five instruments runs from .72 (NEO PI-R) to .92 (BFI). Raw-item PCA finds a sixth component, acquiescence. Within-person centering removes it, and the content-balanced facet scales never produce it. Across 20 self- and peer-reported criteria, BFI-2 facets explain more variance than domains (mean R2 .33 vs .27). The authors stress that facet quality matters more than the number of facets.

Nothing in the paper concerns legislators, lobbying or text. It bears on Paul's systems only through measurement mechanics. (1) The LLM item reader (big5_llm.py) says it uses "balanced keying", but the code keys O, C, E and A at 3 true to 1 false. Only ES is balanced. By the paper's acquiescence logic, a rater that tends to mark items +1 would push O, C, E and A up together and inflate their intercorrelation. The system already worries about this kind of halo. (2) The dormant expert-panel instrument is BFI-2-XS, which takes one item per BFI-2 facet. That panel was CANCELED (see flags). (3) The affective-N LLM read sums pessimism, anxiety, depression and volatility, which roughly match the BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets. In the paper those facets predict different criteria. (4) The self-peer agreement figures give a realistic ceiling for reading convergence between text-based traits and gold ratings. All transfers are indirect: the paper studies general-population self-report, while the system reads politicians' text with LLM and lexical methods. Everything here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: When keying is unbalanced, acquiescent responding acts like a substantive factor. PCA of the 60 raw items gave six components (Big Five plus acquiescence) in both samples. Within-person centering removed the sixth, with congruence of .97 or higher for the remaining five. The content-balanced 15 facet scales gave only five components (eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32, then 0.56 or lower). The mean of raw, unreversed items serves as an acquiescence index (range 1-5).
bearings.paper_location: Study 3 domain- and facet-level structure, pp. 30-31 (Table 6, Table 7, Figure 1); CFA with acquiescence factor pp. 31-34 (Table 8); General Discussion p. 45
bearings.system_side: The Pink LLM reader scores 20 observer items on a -1/0/+1 scale, with 'cannot tell' coded 0. Its docstring says the keying is balanced. In the item table, O, C, E and A each have 3 true-keyed and 1 false-keyed item (O3, C3, E3 and A3 are the only negatives). ES is 2:2. The chunk trait score is the keyed mean sum(s*o[i])/4. A chunk where the model answers +1 to everything therefore scores +0.5 on O, C, E and A but 0 on ES. The CT-CM capstone models a single Pink method factor (halo), which loosely parallels the paper's acquiescence factor, and it MISSed.

bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's mechanism is human self-report yea-saying on a 5-point agree-disagree scale. It carries over only if the LLM has a comparable +1 tendency on observer items. That is plausible but untested, because roughly 90% of answers are expected to be 0 (cue-absent). The fix the paper implies is cheap and diagnostic only. Compute a per-chunk mean of raw, unreversed answers as the acquiescence index, then check its correlation with O, C, E and A, or within-chunk centering. Any item change creates a new ITEMSET_V and cache key. The A-ES halo of about .21 cannot come from acquiescence, because ES is balanced. Treat this as a doc-versus-code discrepancy plus a hypothesis. It stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

Self-peer domain agreement is .42-.69 (mean .56) and facet agreement .27-.73 (mean .49), with peer n = 184 in a student sample. Different Big Five instruments in the same respondents converge at .72-.92.

bearings.paper_claim: Negative Emotionality facets have distinct criterion profiles. Peer-rated stress resistance is predicted by Emotional Volatility (r -.47, beta -.32) and Anxiety (-.46/-.28). Positive relations are predicted by Depression (-.53/-.38). Facets beat domains in mean R2 (.33 vs .27 across 20 criteria; 14/20 criteria with significant incremental R2). The authors add that predictive value depends more on facet quality than on the number of facets.

It is combined with a LIWC-style read, residualized on E and party, and feeds the receptivity N slot. That slot is meant to capture the Byrne pressure-choking mechanism (susc .30 weight).

bearings.transfer_conditions: The pressure mechanism the receptivity layer assumes lines up most closely with Anxiety and Volatility, not with Depression or pessimism. Keeping those components separate is a measurement idea for later, not a recommendation to rewire the engine. Transfer is weak for three reasons. The paper's criteria are general-population self-report and peer ratings of well-being, not legislators' decisions under lobbying pressure. Genre transfer of affective N already failed (rho .050, .161). And no N susceptibility signal has been demonstrated in this system (H5 null). Any facet split would need its own prereg and look.

gaps_exposed: No acquiescence or response-style diagnostic exists for the LLM item reader. The paper's index (mean of raw, unreversed items) and within-person centering are not computed, even though O, C, E and A are keyed 3:1.
The big5_llm.py docstring says 'balanced keying', which contradicts the item table (only ES is 2:2). This is a documentation-integrity gap.

Traits are scored only at the domain level, apart from ad hoc facets (A-antagonism; E communication facets taken from NEO, not BFI-2). There is no hierarchical facet model, so the facet-specific prediction the paper shows (R2 .27 to .33) cannot be tested.

Affective N merges anxiety, depression, volatility and pessimism into one sum. The paper shows these facets predict different criteria, and the receptivity mechanism (pressure-choking) is closest to Anxiety and Volatility.
flags: The expert observer panel (b5_panel_items.py / b5_panel_score.py, BFI-2-XS) was CANCELED by Paul on 2026-07-09 with the instruction never to re-propose it. Nothing here recommends recruiting raters or reviving the panel; the bearing is lineage only.

The keying discrepancy in big5_llm.py and the acquiescence-leak mechanism are new agent analysis. They are UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062). No item change is proposed, because any change to item text or keying creates a new ITEMSET_V and cache.

No graph-rank, revolving-door, LDA-edge or reciprocity wording is involved. The paper argues for neither rejected SNA proposal. Its 'nomological network' is a construct-validity term, not a social network.
Citation check: the system cites Soto & John 2017 JRP 68:69-81 (the BFI-2-XS/S short forms), a separate paper from this JPSP BFI-2 paper. The panel citation is correct and does not need relabelling.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and his psychometrics positions rest on Ramey and Birkenmaier & Lechner. The paper is consistent with his push for validated, codebook-driven trait measurement. It also tempers his receptivity note that '10 personalities collapse into 4 observable ones'. The BFI-2 evidence shows that finer-grained facets add predictive power, but only when each facet is measured reliably, and the system's text-based traits have not reached that level (many single-look MISSes). His notes do not record the canceled panel or the system's halo and method-factor findings, so they are stale on psychometrics validation as built.

Expert observer ratings of senators are the kind of other-rater criterion whose convergence the BFI-2 self-peer figures (mean r .56 domain) help calibrate.
Text-based domain-level Big Five for legislators, which the lexical reader follows. The BFI-2 supplies the hierarchical facet structure and self-report benchmarks that Ramey's approach lacks.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five correlations. Together with the BFI-2 cross-rater and cross-instrument convergence figures, it brackets what text-to-trait convergence can reasonably reach.

Byrne's pressure-choking result is the basis for the receptivity N weight. The BFI-2 facet results (Anxiety and Volatility predict stress resistance; Depression does not) narrow which part of N should carry that mechanism.
